name: Learn: Cluster Operations
objective: CKA › Cluster Architecture, Maintenance & Troubleshooting. Drill EVERY node-level cluster-ops corner harder than the exam: static pods and mirror pods, repairing a crash-looping control-plane component, etcd snapshot backup, node taints and labels, cordon/drain for maintenance, uncordon to return a node, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly on persistent node/cluster state via docker exec and kubectl -o json.
description: Eight strict node-level practicals on a real multi-node kind cluster via docker exec. Node names: $CP (control-plane), $W1/$W2 (workers). Each Check shows which requirements you met and the exact reason for any you missed.

questions.title: Static pod on a worker
questions.teach:
A **static pod** is run by the **kubelet** from a manifest in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on one node — the API server never schedules it. The API shows a read-only **mirror pod** named `<pod>-<node>`.

**Gotcha:** the manifest must live on the node you want the pod on — write it to `$W1`, or no mirror pod appears.
questions.prompt:
On worker node `$W1`, create a static pod named `static-web` (container `web`, image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) by writing a manifest into `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on that node.

Target: the mirror pod `static-web-$W1` is `Running` in namespace `default`, with image `busybox:1.36` and command `sleep 3600`.
questions.hint: In the exam you'd `ssh <node>`; in KindLab that's `docker exec -it $W1 bash`. Then `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/` and create `static-web.yaml` — kind nodes have no vi, so use `cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF' … EOF` — with a Pod named `static-web`. The kubelet forms the mirror pod `static-web-<node>` in ~15s.
questions.solution:
# 1) shell ONTO the worker node (exam equivalent: ssh <node>)
docker exec -it $W1 bash

# 2) now on the node: go to the static-pod dir and create the manifest (use vi in the exam)
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
cat > static-web.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: static-web
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
EOF
exit

# 3) back on the base machine: verify the mirror pod
kubectl get pod static-web-$W1 -n default

verification.description: mirror pod static-web-$W1 Running with image busybox:1.36 + command sleep 3600

questions.title: Repair a crash-looping control-plane component
questions.teach:
The control-plane (apiserver, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd) also runs as **static pods** from `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` on `$CP`. A bad flag crash-loops one; fix the manifest **on the node** and the kubelet restarts it in ~15s.

**Gotcha:** diagnose with `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP` (shows the bad flag); kind nodes have **no vi/nano**, so edit with `sed`, and never `kubectl edit` (mirror pods are read-only).
questions.prompt:
Setup injected a bogus flag into the **kube-scheduler** static pod manifest on `$CP`, so the scheduler crash-loops. Fix `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` so the scheduler becomes healthy.

Target: the `kube-scheduler-$CP` pod in `kube-system` is Ready (1/1) and the bogus flag is gone.
questions.hint: Diagnose: `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP` → `unknown flag: --bogus-flag`. Then shell onto the node (exam: `ssh <node>`; here `docker exec -it $CP bash`), `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, and remove that line with `sed` (no vi on kind nodes). Kubelet restarts it in ~15s.
questions.solution:
# 1) diagnose — the logs name the bad flag
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-scheduler-$CP | tail      # Error: unknown flag: --bogus-flag

# 2) shell onto the control-plane node (exam equivalent: ssh <node>)
docker exec -it $CP bash
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# kind nodes have no vi/nano — edit with sed (or: apt-get update && apt-get install -y vim)
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-scheduler.yaml
exit

# 3) back on base: watch it recover
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-scheduler-$CP -w

verification.description: kube-scheduler static pod Ready again, bogus flag removed

questions.title: Back up etcd
questions.teach:
**etcd** holds all cluster state; back it up with `etcdctl snapshot save`, authenticating via the certs under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/` against `https://127.0.0.1:2379`. Save into `/var/lib/etcd` (mounted on the node), then copy the file out.

**Gotcha:** the etcd image is **distroless — no shell**. Call `etcdctl` directly via `kubectl exec`; wrapping it in `sh -c '...'` fails.
questions.prompt:
Take an etcd snapshot and save it to `/opt/snapshot.db` on the control-plane node `$CP`.

Target: `/opt/snapshot.db` exists on `$CP` and is a real (>1KB) etcd snapshot.
questions.hint: `kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-$CP -- etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db`, then `docker exec $CP cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-"$CP" -- etcdctl \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db
docker exec "$CP" cp /var/lib/etcd/snapshot.db /opt/snapshot.db

verification.description: snapshot is a real (non-trivial, >1KB) etcd backup

questions.title: Taint a node (NoSchedule)
questions.teach:
A **taint** repels pods lacking a matching **toleration**: `kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:effect`. `NoSchedule` blocks new pods that don't tolerate it; it is recorded in the node's `spec.taints`.

**Gotcha:** a taint only affects *scheduling* of new pods — it does NOT evict already-running pods (that behavior is `NoExecute`).
questions.prompt:
Taint worker node `$W1` so ordinary pods won't schedule there: key `workload`, value `batch`, effect `NoSchedule`.

Target: `$W1` has a taint `workload=batch:NoSchedule` in `spec.taints`.
questions.hint: `kubectl taint nodes $W1 workload=batch:NoSchedule`. Inspect with `kubectl get node $W1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.taints}'`.

questions.title: Cordon and drain a node
questions.teach:
To prep a node for maintenance, `kubectl cordon` sets `spec.unschedulable=true` (no *new* pods); `kubectl drain` then evicts existing pods (and cordons automatically). Pass `--ignore-daemonsets` and `--delete-emptydir-data`.

**Gotcha:** without those two flags, drain refuses — read the error, add the flag, rerun.
questions.prompt:
Node `$W2` needs maintenance. Cordon it, then drain it (ignoring DaemonSets and deleting emptyDir data).

Target: `$W2` is cordoned — `spec.unschedulable=true` — and the drain completed.

questions.title: Uncordon the control-plane
questions.teach:
`kubectl uncordon <node>` reverses a cordon, setting `spec.unschedulable=false` to return the node to service. It does **not** pull back pods that drain evicted — the scheduler places *new* pods there over time.

**Gotcha:** `uncordon` takes a **node** name (not a pod) and is idempotent — running it on a schedulable node is a no-op.
questions.prompt:
The control-plane node `$CP` was cordoned for maintenance. Bring it back into service.

Target: `$CP` is schedulable again — `spec.unschedulable` is not `true`.

questions.title: Label a node
questions.teach:
Node **labels** are `key=value` metadata used by `nodeSelector`/affinity to steer scheduling. Add one with `kubectl label node <node> key=value`; replace an existing key with `--overwrite`.

**Gotcha:** labels (`metadata.labels`, for selection) are NOT taints (`spec.taints`, for repelling) — this step wants a label.
questions.prompt:
Label worker node `$W2` with `disk=ssd` so a storage workload can target it.

Target: `$W2` has label `disk=ssd` in `metadata.labels`.
questions.hint: `kubectl label node $W2 disk=ssd`. Check with `kubectl get node $W2 --show-labels` or `-o jsonpath='{.metadata.labels.disk}'`.

questions.title: Diagnose & fix: a crash-looping controller-manager (no hint)
questions.teach:
When a control-plane component is unhealthy, `kubectl -n kube-system get pods` shows the crash-looping one; its logs or its manifest on `$CP` reveal the cause. Fix the manifest on the node and let the kubelet restart it.

**Gotcha:** the fault is a bad flag in the manifest — no hint here; find it yourself, then confirm the pod reaches `1/1 Ready`.
questions.prompt:
Setup has broken the **kube-controller-manager** static pod on `$CP`; it is crash-looping. Diagnose the cause and fix it so the component is healthy again. Edit the manifest on the node — do not try `kubectl edit`.

Target: `kube-controller-manager-$CP` in `kube-system` is Ready (1/1).
questions.hint: No hint on the fault — diagnose it: `kubectl -n kube-system get pods` shows the crash; `kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP` (or `crictl logs` on the node) names the cause. Fix the manifest on `$CP` with `sed` (kind has no vi): shell in, `cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/`, remove the bad line.
questions.solution:
# diagnose: logs name the bad flag
kubectl -n kube-system logs kube-controller-manager-$CP | tail    # unknown flag: --bogus-flag

# fix on the node (no vi on kind -> sed)
docker exec -it $CP bash
cd /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
grep -n bogus kube-controller-manager.yaml
sed -i '/--bogus-flag=true/d' kube-controller-manager.yaml
exit

kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-controller-manager-$CP -w

verification.description: kube-controller-manager static pod Ready again, fault removed
